summary: Moon Compass is a web tool that shows whether a lunar landing site and date give a lander sunlight for power and a direct link to Earth, and for how long. It uses real NASA LOLA terrain for south-pole sites, checks NASA Deep Space Network visibility, gives an instant GO/NO-GO, compares site and date options side by side, and finds the best landing windows. Its Sun and Earth positions match NASA's Apollo records to within 0.2 degrees. A short launch slip can halve a polar mission's sunlight.
details:
Moon Compass is a web tool that tells mission planners, in seconds, whether a lunar landing site and date will give a lander sunlight for power and a direct line of sight to Earth for communication, and for how long.

WHAT IT DOES

- Site selection: 18 curated landing sites (Apollo 11-17, CLPS landers IM-1, IM-2 and Blue Ghost, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, Chang'e 3-6, Mons Mouton, the south pole and Shackleton crater), plus any custom coordinates or a click on the south-polar map.

- Date and time flexibility: any UTC date and time. One click "slips" a scenario by a day or a week, the typical question after a launch delay.

- Sun and Earth visualization: a horizon panorama shows the Sun and Earth at their true angular sizes against the real terrain skyline, with their paths across the coming mission days.

- Power and communication metrics: solar elevation and azimuth, how much of the solar disk clears the terrain, a relative solar-array power index, Earth elevation and azimuth, time to sunset/sunrise and Earthset/Earthrise, share of the mission sunlit, share with a direct Earth link, and the longest continuous power + link window.

- Instant verdict: GO / MARGINAL / NO-GO, with plain-language reasons, for up to four site/date scenarios side by side.

- Landing-date finder: scans 90 days of start times for the chosen mission length and highlights every GO window. Click a bar to load that date.

- Temporal dynamics: 30-day timelines for each scenario, and a Play button that animates a full lunar day at all sites at once.

- South-polar map: every point from 60°S (or 80°S) to the pole is coloured by Sun and Earth visibility at the chosen time, showing why a few kilometres can change everything.

- Deep Space Network check: a direct link also requires Goldstone, Madrid or Canberra to see the Moon above 10°. Contact gaps are flagged.

HOW IT WORKS

Sun and Moon positions come from the open-source Astronomy Engine ephemeris (validated by its author against JPL Horizons). They are rotated into the Moon's body-fixed frame with the IAU lunar rotation model, so libration is included. Elevation and azimuth are then computed for an observer on the lunar surface, including parallax. The Moon has no atmosphere, so the horizon is pure geometry.

For the south-polar sites we use real NASA terrain. From NASA's LRO Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter elevation map (LDEM_75S_240M), we traced 250 km in each of 360 directions from every site, including lunar curvature, to get its true horizon. The Sun and Earth are tested against the terrain in their own direction.

VALIDATION

- Sun and Earth positions match the values in NASA's Apollo Lunar Surface Journal for Apollo 11, 12 and 14: within 0.02° for the Sun and 0.18° for Earth.

- With LOLA terrain, the predicted sunset at IM-1's landing site moves 1.3 days earlier than on a smooth Moon, toward Odysseus' actual loss of power on 29 Feb 2024 at the start of lunar night.

- Shackleton's crater floor gets 0% sunlight over all of 2026, consistent with it being a permanently shadowed region.

All checks run live inside the app.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

South-pole missions are extremely sensitive to schedule changes. At IM-2's Mons Mouton site, landing on 16 Nov 2026 gives a 10-day mission 100% sunlight, while landing on 26 Nov gives only 50%. Moon Compass lets planners re-screen sites and dates in minutes when hardware or launch dates slip, gives science and engineering teams one shared picture of power and communication trade-offs, and helps students and the public see why the lunar poles are so different from anywhere on Earth.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

It turns expert ephemeris and terrain data into a single "GO / NO-GO" answer anyone can read. It shows the lander's actual sky with true-size Sun and Earth over the real skyline. It runs entirely in the browser, with no install or account needed.

TOOLS

HTML, JavaScript and Canvas; Astronomy Engine (MIT licence); NASA LOLA topography processed in JavaScript; Python for testing.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy (checked against NASA records), honesty about limits, and speed of comparison. Known limits: the 240 m terrain map misses small nearby craters and boulders, and LOLA horizons are precomputed only for the named south-polar sites; clicked points use a smooth-Moon or preset horizon. Next steps: on-demand LOLA horizons for any point, NASA's 5 m landing-site elevation maps, relay-orbiter link windows, and night-length (thermal) metrics.
